steps.body: Remember shapes as members-only clubs with entry rules? A **rectangle's** entry rule is angle-based: **all four angles must be exactly 90°.** A quadrilateral missing that rule — even by one angle — doesn't get into the rectangle club, though it's still a quadrilateral.
Build a rectangle from angle and parallel-side attributes.

widget.prompt: Build a rectangle: four sides, four right angles, and two pairs of parallel sides. Equal sides are not required for the rectangle rule.
widget.successFeedback: The rectangle rule is satisfied: four right angles force two pairs of parallel opposite sides.
widget.sidesFeedback: A rectangle is a quadrilateral, so it must have four sides.
widget.attributesFeedback: Focus on four right angles and two parallel pairs. Equal sides would make a special rectangle—a square.

options.label: No — the fourth gets forced to 90° too
Yes — easily

predict.reveal: Four angles must total 360° — three right angles spend 270°, leaving exactly 90° for the last. Three rights smuggle in a fourth.

options.label: They satisfy the same defining rules.
options.feedback: Yes — orientation and size are irrelevant to membership.

options.feedback: A family includes every shape satisfying its rules.

explanationVariants: A shape needs ALL FOUR angles at exactly 90° to join the rectangle club — three isn't enough.
The entry rule has no partial credit.

options.label: No club membership — one angle fails the entry rule
options.feedback: The rectangle's rule requires ALL FOUR angles at 90° — even one exception fails entry.

options.label: Yes — three out of four is close enough
options.feedback: The entry rule doesn't allow exceptions. Even one angle short of 90° means it's not a rectangle.

options.label: Yes — 85° rounds to 90°
options.feedback: Angles don't round for club membership — the rule is exactly 90°, and 85° falls short.

options.label: It depends on the shape's size
options.feedback: Size never matters for entry rules — only the actual angle measures do, and one angle here misses 90°.

steps.body: A quadrilateral can have **any number** of right angles — zero, one, two, or four (never exactly three, since the fourth would then be forced to also equal 90° by the shape's angle total). Fewer than four just means a different family, not a failed shape.

explanationVariants: A general quadrilateral with no special structure can easily have zero right angles.
Not joining the rectangle club doesn't disqualify it from being a quadrilateral at all.

widget.prompt: A four-sided shape has no angles that measure exactly 90°. Is it still a valid quadrilateral?

options.label: Yes — quadrilateral only requires 4 sides, not any right angles
options.feedback: Being a quadrilateral just means having 4 sides. Right angles are the SEPARATE rectangle entry rule.

options.label: No — every quadrilateral needs at least one right angle
options.feedback: There's no such requirement. A quadrilateral just needs 4 sides — right angles are only the rectangle club's rule.

options.label: No — it must be some other kind of shape entirely
options.feedback: A 4-sided shape is a quadrilateral regardless of its angles. It's just not in the rectangle family specifically.

options.label: Only if all four sides are equal length
options.feedback: Side length isn't part of the basic quadrilateral rule either — 4 sides is enough. This shape qualifies.

explanationVariants: If three angles are each 90°, they already total 270°; the fourth must be 360−270=90° too — forcing all four.
A quadrilateral's angles always total 360°, which makes exactly three right angles impossible.

widget.prompt: Could a quadrilateral have EXACTLY three right angles (and a fourth angle that isn't 90°)?

options.label: No — the fourth angle would be forced to be 90° too
options.feedback: Three 90° angles total 270°; since all four must total 360°, the fourth is forced to be exactly 90° as well.

options.label: Yes — the fourth angle could be anything
options.feedback: It can't be just anything — the four angles must total 360°. Three 90° angles leave exactly 90° for the fourth, forcing it too.

options.label: Yes, if the quadrilateral is large enough
options.feedback: Size doesn't change the angle total — every quadrilateral's angles sum to 360°, forcing the fourth angle to be 90° here.

options.label: Only for certain irregular shapes
options.feedback: The 360° total applies to every quadrilateral without exception, forcing the fourth angle to be 90° whenever the other three are.

options.feedback: Even one corner short of exactly 90° means this frame doesn't meet the rectangle's entry rule.

options.feedback: The rectangle rule allows no exceptions. One corner at 88° means this isn't a true rectangle.

options.label: Yes — 88° is basically 90°
options.feedback: The entry rule is exact, not approximate. 88° falls short of the required 90°, so this frame fails entry.

options.label: It depends on the frame's overall size
options.feedback: Size is irrelevant here — the exact angle measures decide it, and 88° isn't 90°.

takeaways: A rectangle's entry rule requires all four angles to be exactly 90°.
A quadrilateral can have 0, 1, 2, or 4 right angles — never exactly 3, since the fourth is then forced.
Failing one club's entry rule never disqualifies a shape from being a quadrilateral at all.

The rectangle entry rule allows zero exceptions.
